chapters.title: Yaʿqūb and his two transmitters
paragraphs: The reader: Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Ḥaḍramī al-Baṣrī (d. 205 AH) is the ninth of the ten readers. He led the reciters of Baṣrah after Abū ʿAmr.
The transmitters: Ruways (Muḥammad ibn al-Mutawakkil al-Baṣrī, d. 238 AH) and Rawḥ (Abū al-Ḥasan Rawḥ ibn ʿAbd al-Muʾmin al-Hudhalī al-Baṣrī, d. 235 AH).

The way: these rules follow al-Durrah al-Muḍiyyah of Ibn al-Jazarī. The poem treats Abū ʿAmr al-Baṣrī as the basis (aṣl) of Yaʿqūb and mentions only the places where Yaʿqūb, or one of his transmitters, leaves him. Its symbols are ḥāʾ for Yaʿqūb, ṭāʾ for Ruways and yāʾ for Rawḥ. In general Rawḥ is the closer of the two to Ḥafṣ.

chapters.title: Istiʿādhah and basmalah
paragraphs: Istiʿādhah: Yaʿqūb has no rule of his own here; its wording and manner are the same as for the other readers.

Between two sūrahs: three choices are allowed. The first is the basmalah in its three accepted forms: stopping on both sides of it (preferred), stopping before it and joining it to the next sūrah, or joining everything. The second is sakt, a short pause without breath and without basmalah. The third is waṣl, joining the two sūrahs without basmalah. Sakt comes before waṣl in preference. Ḥafṣ has only the basmalah.
Al-Anfāl to al-Tawbah: there is no basmalah; the two sūrahs are linked by sakt or by waṣl, as for every reader.
Verse count: Yaʿqūb does not count the basmalah as an āyah, and he follows the Baṣran count of verses.

chapters.title: The hāʾ of the plural and dual pronouns, and mīm al-jamʿ
paragraphs: Mīm al-jamʿ before a vowelled letter: it is sākinah, with no ṣilah, as in the reading of Ḥafṣ.

Hāʾ after a sākin yāʾ: the hāʾ of the pronouns هُمْ, هُمَا and هُنَّ takes a ḍammah whenever a sākin yāʾ comes before it, whether a yāʾ of madd or of līn, in waṣl and in waqf: عَلَيْهُمْ, فِيهُمْ, وَيُزَكِّيهُمْ, إِلَيْهُنَّ, عَلَيْهُمَا. Ḥafṣ reads a kasrah in all of these.

What is not included: a hāʾ not preceded by a yāʾ (رَبِّهِمْ, بِهِنَّ, بِهِمَا), a hāʾ after a vowelled yāʾ (مِنْ حُلِيِّهِمْ, 7:148), and the singular pronoun (عَلَيْهِ, إِلَيْهِ, لَدَيْهِ). These keep the kasrah.

Ruways, the dropped yāʾ: where the sākin yāʾ before the pronoun has fallen away because the verb is majzūm or an imperative, Ruways still reads the hāʾ with ḍammah. There are fifteen places: 7:38, 7:169, 7:203, 9:14, 9:70, 10:39, 15:3, 20:133, 24:32, 29:51, 33:68, 37:11, 37:149, 40:7 and 40:9. Examples: فَآتِهُمْ عَذَابًا (7:38), أَوَلَمْ يَكْفِهُمْ (29:51), وَقِهُمْ عَذَابَ الْجَحِيمِ (40:7). The one exception is وَمَن يُوَلِّهِمْ (8:16), read with kasrah. Rawḥ reads the hāʾ with kasrah in all of these places.

Mīm al-jamʿ before a sākin letter: the mīm takes the same vowel as the hāʾ before it. After a sākin yāʾ both carry ḍammah: عَلَيْهُمُ الْقِتَالُ, يُرِيهُمُ اللَّهُ, إِلَيْهُمُ اثْنَيْنِ. After a kasrah both carry kasrah: بِهِمِ الْأَسْبَابُ, مِن دُونِهِمِ امْرَأَتَيْنِ. Ḥafṣ reads عَلَيْهِمُ and بِهِمُ. In Ruways's fifteen places the same holds: وَيُلْهِهُمُ الْأَمَلُ (15:3), يُغْنِهُمُ اللَّهُ (24:32), وَقِهُمُ السَّيِّئَاتِ (40:9).

chapters.title: Hāʾ al-kināyah
paragraphs: Read short by both transmitters: the hāʾ has its vowel without ṣilah in يُؤَدِّهِ (3:75, twice), نُؤْتِهِ (3:145, 42:20), نُوَلِّهِ and وَنُصْلِهِ (4:115), وَيَتَّقِهِ (24:52), فَأَلْقِهِ (27:28), يَرْضَهُ (39:7) and فِيهِ مُهَانًا (25:69). In the last one Ḥafṣ reads with ṣilah.
Where the transmitters differ: in يَأْتِهِ (20:75) and in بِيَدِهِ (2:237, 2:249, 23:88, 36:83) Ruways reads the hāʾ short, while Rawḥ reads it with ṣilah.
Kasrah where Ḥafṣ has ḍammah: وَمَا أَنسَانِيهِ (18:63) and عَلَيْهِ اللَّهَ (48:10) are read with a kasrah on the hāʾ.
Arjiʾhu: أَرْجِئْهُ (7:111, 26:36) is read with a sākin hamzah after the jīm and a short ḍammah on the hāʾ, without ṣilah. Ḥafṣ reads أَرْجِهْ.

chapters.title: Idghām kabīr
paragraphs: Taʾmannā: لَا تَأْمَنَّا (12:11) is read with idghām together with rawm or ishmām.

Yaʿqūb, both transmitters: two identical vowelled letters are merged in three places: وَالصَّاحِب بِّالْجَنبِ (4:36), أَتُمِدُّونِّي (27:36) and رَبِّكَ تَّمَارَىٰ (53:55). The last is only in waṣl; beginning with the verb, he pronounces both tāʾs. Ḥafṣ reads all three with iẓhār.

Ruways, without khulf: kāf into kāf in نُسَبِّحَك كَّثِيرًا (20:33), وَنَذْكُرَك كَّثِيرًا (20:34) and إِنَّك كُّنتَ (20:35); bāʾ into bāʾ in فَلَا أَنسَاب بَّيْنَهُمْ (23:101); tāʾ into tāʾ in ثُمَّ تَّفَكَّرُوا (34:46). This last one is likewise only in waṣl.

Ruways, with khulf: he has two ways, idghām and iẓhār, with idghām given first, in جَعَل لَّكُم, eight times in al-Naḥl (16:72 twice, 16:78, 16:80 twice, 16:81 three times); in وَأَنَّه هُّوَ, four times in al-Najm (53:43, 53:44, 53:48, 53:49); in لَذَهَب بِّسَمْعِهِمْ (2:20), الْكِتَاب بِّأَيْدِيهُمْ (2:79) and الْكِتَاب بِّالْحَقِّ (2:176); and in لَا قِبَل لَّهُم (27:37).
Rawḥ: in all of the places special to Ruways he reads with iẓhār, as Ḥafṣ does.

chapters.title: Madd and qaṣr, and leaving sakt
paragraphs: Madd munfaṣil: qaṣr, two ḥarakāt, as in بِمَا أُنزِلَ. Ḥafṣ lengthens it.
Madd muttaṣil: tawassuṭ, four ḥarakāt.
Madd badal and līn: the badal is two ḥarakāt, as in آمَنُوا, إِيمَانًا, أُوتُوا, and a līn letter before a hamzah gets no added length, as in شَيْءٍ and سَوْءَةَ. This is the same as Ḥafṣ.
The word anā: in waṣl the alif of أَنَا is dropped before a hamzat al-qaṭʿ, whether maftūḥah or maḍmūmah, as in أَنَا أَوَّلُ and أَنَا أُحْيِي, so there is no madd.

No sakt: the four places where Ḥafṣ pauses are read straight through in waṣl: عِوَجًا قَيِّمًا (18:1–2) with ikhfāʾ of the tanwīn, مِن مَّرْقَدِنَا هَٰذَا (36:52) joined, and مَن رَّاقٍ (75:27) and بَل رَّانَ (83:14) with idghām.

chapters.title: Two hamzahs in one word
paragraphs: General rule: no alif of idkhāl is put between the two hamzahs, unlike Abū ʿAmr. Ruways reads the second hamzah with tashīl; Rawḥ reads both with taḥqīq, as Ḥafṣ does. This holds whether the second hamzah is maftūḥah, maḍmūmah or maksūrah: ءَأَنذَرْتَهُمْ, أَؤُنَبِّئُكُم, أَئِنَّكُمْ.
Aʾimmah: Ruways reads أَئِمَّةَ with tashīl of the second hamzah and no idkhāl.
Āmantum: in the three places of ءَامَنتُمْ (7:123, 20:71, 26:49) Ruways reads a statement with a single hamzah, like Ḥafṣ. Rawḥ reads a question, with two fully pronounced hamzahs.

Words read as a question: Yaʿqūb reads with two hamzahs in أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجَالَ (7:81), أَئِنَّ لَنَا (7:113), أَئِنَّكَ لَأَنتَ يُوسُفُ (12:90), أَأَذْهَبْتُمْ (46:20) and أَأَن كَانَ ذَا مَالٍ (68:14). Ḥafṣ has a single hamzah in all of these except 12:90. Ruways eases the second hamzah and Rawḥ pronounces both.
Al-siḥr: بِهِ السِّحْرُ (10:81) is read without a question hamzah, as Ḥafṣ reads it.

The repeated question (istifhām mukarrar): in nine places Yaʿqūb reads the first phrase as a question and the second as a statement, as in أَئِذَا كُنَّا تُرَابًا إِنَّا لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ (13:5). The others are 17:49, 17:98, 23:82, 32:10, 37:16, 37:53, 56:47 and 79:10–11. In al-ʿAnkabūt (29:28–29) the first is a statement and the second a question: إِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الْفَاحِشَةَ then أَئِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجَالَ. In al-Naml (27:67) the second phrase, أَئِنَّا لَمُخْرَجُونَ, is a question. Wherever two hamzahs meet, Ruways eases the second and Rawḥ pronounces both.

chapters.title: Two hamzahs in two words
paragraphs: Scope: the rule applies only in waṣl, when a word ending in a hamzah is joined to a word beginning with one.
Rawḥ: he reads both hamzahs with taḥqīq in every case, like Ḥafṣ.
Ruways, same vowel: he reads the second hamzah with tashīl, as in جَاءَ أَمْرُنَا, مِنَ السَّمَاءِ إِن and أَوْلِيَاءُ أُولَٰئِكَ.

Ruways, different vowels: he follows Abū ʿAmr. When the first is maftūḥah and the second maksūrah or maḍmūmah, the second has tashīl: تَفِيءَ إِلَىٰ, جَاءَ أُمَّةً. When the first is maḍmūmah and the second maftūḥah, the second becomes a pure wāw (ibdāl): نَشَاءُ أَصَبْنَاهُم. When the first is maksūrah and the second maftūḥah, the second becomes a pure yāʾ: مِنَ السَّمَاءِ أَوِ ائْتِنَا. When the first is maḍmūmah and the second maksūrah, he has two ways, tashīl or ibdāl into a wāw: يَشَاءُ إِلَىٰ.

chapters.title: The single hamzah and naql
paragraphs: Sākin hamzah: Yaʿqūb pronounces it fully wherever it stands in the word, as in يُؤْمِنُونَ, الذِّئْبُ and اقْرَأْ. This agrees with Ḥafṣ.
Words read with a hamzah: كُفُؤًا (112:4), هُزُؤًا, زَكَرِيَّاءَ, تُرْجِئُ (33:51), مُرْجَئُونَ (9:106) and لَا يَأْلِتْكُم (49:14). Ḥafṣ reads none of these with a hamzah.
Words read without a hamzah: يَاجُوجَ وَمَاجُوجَ (18:94, 21:96) with an alif in place of the hamzah, and يُضَاهُونَ (9:30) with the hamzah dropped. Ḥafṣ has a hamzah in both.
Al-lāʾi: اللَّاءِ (33:4, 58:2, 65:4) is read with a fully pronounced hamzah maksūrah and no yāʾ after it. Ḥafṣ reads اللَّائِي.

Naql: Yaʿqūb does not move the vowel of a hamzah onto the sākin before it, except in عَادًا الْأُولَىٰ (53:50), which he reads عَادًا لُّولَىٰ: the ḍammah passes to the lām, the hamzah falls away and the tanwīn merges into the lām. If he stops on عَادًا and begins the next word, three ways are allowed: اَلُولَىٰ (given first), لُولَىٰ, or the original form الْأُولَىٰ.
Ruways, istabraq: he makes naql in مِنْ إِسْتَبْرَقٍ (55:54), reading مِنِ اسْتَبْرَقٍ. Rawḥ reads it without naql.

chapters.title: Idghām and iẓhār
paragraphs: Idh, qad, the feminine tāʾ, hal and bal: Yaʿqūb reads the dhāl of idh, the dāl of qad, the tāʾ of the feminine and the lām of hal and bal with iẓhār before all their letters, leaving Abū ʿAmr and agreeing with Ḥafṣ. This includes هَلْ تَرَىٰ (67:3, 69:8).
Bāʾ majzūmah before fāʾ: iẓhār in its five places, such as أَوْ يَغْلِبْ فَسَوْفَ (4:74) and وَإِن تَعْجَبْ فَعَجَبٌ (13:5); the others are 17:63, 20:97 and 49:11.
Rāʾ majzūmah before lām: iẓhār, as in يَغْفِرْ لَكُمْ and وَاصْبِرْ لِحُكْمِ.

Other words with iẓhār: فَنَبَذْتُهَا (20:96), عُذْتُ (40:27, 44:20), لَبِثْتَ and لَبِثْتُمْ in all their forms, أُورِثْتُمُوهَا (7:43, 43:72), يُرِدْ ثَوَابَ (3:145, both times), and the ṣād of كهيعص before ذِكْرُ (19:1–2). Ḥafṣ reads the same.
Words with idghām: يَلْهَث ذَّٰلِكَ (7:176), thāʾ into dhāl, and ارْكَب مَّعَنَا (11:42), bāʾ into mīm.
Yā-Sīn and Nūn: in waṣl the nūn at the end of the letter name is merged into the wāw in يسٓ وَالْقُرْآنِ (36:1–2) and نٓ وَالْقَلَمِ (68:1). Ḥafṣ reads both with iẓhār.

Akhadhtu and ittakhadhtum: in this family of words (أَخَذْتُمْ, اتَّخَذْتُمْ, اتَّخَذْتَ, أَخَذْتُهَا) the two transmitters differ. One merges the dhāl into the tāʾ and the other reads it clearly as Ḥafṣ does. The sources do not agree on which transmitter has which; see the doubts.

chapters.title: Fatḥ and imālah
paragraphs: General rule: Yaʿqūb reads with fatḥ. Imālah is found in a few words only.
Aʿmā: both transmitters read the first أَعْمَىٰ in وَمَن كَانَ فِي هَٰذِهِ أَعْمَىٰ (17:72) with imālah. The second one in the same āyah has fatḥ.
Kāfirīn: Ruways reads كَافِرِينَ and الْكَافِرِينَ with imālah wherever they occur. Rawḥ has imālah only in مِن قَوْمٍ كَافِرِينَ (27:43) and fatḥ everywhere else.
Yā-Sīn: Rawḥ reads the yāʾ of يسٓ (36:1) with imālah; Ruways reads it with fatḥ.
Majrāhā: Yaʿqūb has no imālah here. He reads مُجْرَاهَا (11:41) with a ḍammah on the mīm and a plain fatḥah on the rāʾ, whereas Ḥafṣ reads مَجْرَاهَا with imālah.

chapters.title: Waqf
paragraphs: Feminine tāʾ written open: on words such as رَحْمَتَ, نِعْمَتَ and امْرَأَتَ he stops with a sākin hāʾ, following Abū ʿAmr, where Ḥafṣ stops with a tāʾ. Five are excepted and stopped on with tāʾ: ذَاتَ بَهْجَةٍ, وَلَاتَ, مَرْضَاتِ, هَيْهَاتَ and اللَّاتَ.
Hāʾ al-sakt on the question mā: when the alif of mā has dropped after a preposition he adds a sākin hāʾ in waqf: لِمَهْ, فِيمَهْ, مِمَّهْ, عَمَّهْ, بِمَهْ.
Hāʾ al-sakt on huwa and hiya: he stops هُوَهْ and هِيَهْ, also after wāw, fāʾ or lām: وَهُوَهْ, فَهِيَهْ, لَهُوَهْ.

Hāʾ al-sakt on the feminine plural hunna: he adds it after the doubled nūn of the pronoun, whether joined to a verb, a noun or a particle: عَلَيْهُنَّهْ, لَهُنَّهْ, بُيُوتِهِنَّهْ. It is not added to a doubled nūn that is not this pronoun (وَلَا يَحْزَنَّ) nor after kāf or tāʾ (مِنكُنَّ, كُنتُنَّ). The scholars differ over مِن كَيْدِكُنَّ (12:28).
Hāʾ al-sakt on the doubled yāʾ of the speaker: عَلَيَّهْ, لَدَيَّهْ, بِيَدَيَّهْ, بِمُصْرِخِيَّهْ.

Ruways only: he adds hāʾ al-sakt on words of lament, يَا أَسَفَاهْ and يَا حَسْرَتَاهْ, with full madd of the alif before the sākin hāʾ, and on the adverb ثَمَّ, read ثَمَّهْ. Rawḥ stops on these without a hāʾ.

The written hāʾ al-sakt: in its seven words, يَتَسَنَّهْ (2:259), اقْتَدِهْ (6:90), كِتَابِيَهْ, حِسَابِيَهْ, مَالِيَهْ, سُلْطَانِيَهْ (al-Ḥāqqah) and مَا هِيَهْ (101:10), Yaʿqūb drops the hāʾ in waṣl and keeps it in waqf. Ḥafṣ keeps it in both.

A yāʾ dropped in the rasm before a sākin: he restores the yāʾ in waqf in seventeen places: 2:269, 4:146, 5:3, 6:57, 10:103, 20:12, 22:54, 27:18, 28:30, 30:53, 36:23, 37:163, 50:41, 54:5, 55:24, 79:16 and 81:16. Examples: وَادِ النَّمْلِ stopped as وَادِي, يُنَادِ الْمُنَادِ as يُنَادِي, الْجَوَارِ الْمُنشَآتُ as الْجَوَارِي. Ḥafṣ stops without the yāʾ. A yāʾ dropped because of tanwīn, as in هَادٍ and وَالٍ, is not restored.

Other stops: on أَيُّهَ (24:31, 43:49, 55:31) he stops with an alif, أَيُّهَا; on وَكَأَيِّن he stops on the yāʾ; on وَيْكَأَنَّ and وَيْكَأَنَّهُ (28:82) he stops at the end of the word; on فَمَالِ and مَالِ (4:78, 18:49, 25:7, 70:36) he stops on the lām. In أَيًّا مَّا تَدْعُوا (17:110) Ruways stops on أَيًّا.

chapters.title: Yāʾāt al-iḍāfah
paragraphs: General rule: Yaʿqūb reads the yāʾ of the speaker sākinah in all its categories, apart from what follows.

Before lām al-taʿrīf: in waṣl he reads the yāʾ with fatḥah, as in رَبِّيَ الَّذِي. Two vocative cases are excepted and read sākinah: يَا عِبَادِي الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا (29:56) and يَا عِبَادِي الَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا (39:53).
Qul li-ʿibādī: in قُل لِّعِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا (14:31) Ruways reads the yāʾ with fatḥah in waṣl and Rawḥ reads it sākinah. In waqf both have it sākinah.
Two further fatḥahs: وَمَحْيَايَ (6:162) and مِن بَعْدِيَ اسْمُهُ (61:6). In the second, Ḥafṣ has a sākin yāʾ.
Qawmī: in إِنَّ قَوْمِي اتَّخَذُوا (25:30) Ruways reads the yāʾ sākinah and Rawḥ reads it with fatḥah, قَوْمِيَ اتَّخَذُوا.
Yā ʿibādi: in يَا عِبَادِ لَا خَوْفٌ (43:68) Ruways reads a sākin yāʾ, يَا عِبَادِي, and Rawḥ leaves the yāʾ out, as Ḥafṣ does.

chapters.title: Yāʾāt al-zawāʾid
paragraphs: General rule: Yaʿqūb pronounces the yāʾ that is absent from the rasm in both states, waṣl and waqf, in well over a hundred places. Ḥafṣ leaves nearly all of them out.

At the ends of āyāt: فَارْهَبُونِ (2:40) is read فَارْهَبُونِي, وَأَطِيعُونِ (3:50) is read وَأَطِيعُونِي, and مَتَابِ (13:30) is read مَتَابِي. The same holds for the like of دُعَاءِ (14:40), وَعِيدِ (50:14), نَذِيرِ (67:17), أَكْرَمَنِ (89:15) and دِينِ (109:6).
Within āyāt: الدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ (2:186) is read الدَّاعِي إِذَا دَعَانِي, يَوْمَ يَأْتِ (11:105) is read يَأْتِي, and الْمُهْتَدِ (17:97, 18:17) is read الْمُهْتَدِي.
Ātāni: in فَمَا آتَانِ اللَّهُ (27:36) both transmitters pronounce the yāʾ in waqf. In waṣl only Ruways keeps it, آتَانِيَ اللَّهُ.
Yā ʿibādi fa-ttaqūn: the yāʾ of يَا عِبَادِ (39:16) is pronounced by Ruways alone.
Fa-bashshir ʿibādi: in فَبَشِّرْ عِبَادِ (39:17) the yāʾ is pronounced in waqf and falls away in waṣl because of the sākin that follows.
Not included: يَرْتَعْ (12:12), which Yaʿqūb reads with a sākin ʿayn, and مَن يَتَّقِ (12:90) have no added yāʾ in his reading.

chapters.title: Notable individual words
paragraphs: Mālik: مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ (1:4) is read with an alif, as Ḥafṣ reads it and unlike Abū ʿAmr.
Ṣirāṭ: Ruways reads it with a sīn wherever it occurs, السِّرَاطَ and سِرَاطَ. Rawḥ reads it with a ṣād, like Ḥafṣ.
Arinā and arinī: Yaʿqūb reads the rāʾ sākinah, أَرْنَا and أَرْنِي, where Ḥafṣ has a kasrah.
Turahhibūna: Ruways reads تُرَهِّبُونَ (8:60) with a fatḥah on the rāʾ and a doubled hāʾ.
Lā khawfa: Yaʿqūb reads لَا خَوْفَ عَلَيْهُمْ with a fatḥah on the fāʾ and no tanwīn, and with the ḍammah on the hāʾ described above.
Li-yahaba: لِيَهَبَ لَكِ (19:19) is read with a yāʾ, where Ḥafṣ reads لِأَهَبَ with a hamzah.
Dakkā: in al-Kahf (18:98) he reads دَكًّا with tanwīn and no hamzah, where Ḥafṣ reads دَكَّاءَ.
Allā tattakhidhū: أَلَّا تَتَّخِذُوا (17:2) is read by both transmitters in the second person, as Ḥafṣ reads it and unlike Abū ʿAmr.

doubts: Akhadhtu / ittakhadhtum: the Durrah study (p. 55) says Ruways merges the dhāl into the tāʾ and Rawḥ reads iẓhār, but rules-of-the-10-qiraat lists this idghām among Rawḥ's places (its other line on Ruways is garbled). The Durrah's own wording is usually explained as iẓhār for Ruways and idghām for Rawḥ. The chapter therefore states only that the two transmitters differ; this needs checking against a reliable muṣḥaf of each riwāyah.

Repeated question in al-Naml 27:67: the Durrah study says the first phrase is a statement and the second a question (as in al-ʿAnkabūt), while El-Ibyari says Yaʿqūb reads a question in both phrases in al-Naml. Only the second phrase is stated in the chapter.

Ruways's idghām kabīr with khulf: the Durrah study gives idghām as the preferred way in all of these places; El-Ibyari's table seems to prefer iẓhār for الكتاب بالحق (2:176) and has an unclear remark about 2:79. El-Ibyari also quotes al-Naḥḥās as reading Ruways's idghām without khulf and adding جهنم مهاد (7:41); this was left out.

Rawḥ's mīm in وقهم السيئات, يغنهم الله and ويلههم الأمل: by the general rule of the Durrah study the mīm follows the kasrah of the hāʾ, and El-Ibyari lists وَقِهِمِ السَّيِّئَاتِ that way, but the same book also says in another line that Rawḥ reads these with a ḍammah on the mīm. The chapter states only Rawḥ's kasrah on the hāʾ.

Yāʾ al-iḍāfah before lām al-taʿrīf: the Durrah study and El-Ibyari's table give fatḥah with a few sākin exceptions; rules-of-the-10-qiraat words it the other way round (sukūn except the two يا عبادي الذين). The chapter follows the first two. The Durrah study gives no example word; رَبِّيَ الَّذِي is the example of the category used in rules-of-the-10-qiraat.

Hāʾ al-sakt for Ruways: the Durrah study and El-Ibyari give ثَمَّ and the words of lament to Ruways only; rules-of-the-10-qiraat attributes ثَمَّ to Yaʿqūb as a whole. El-Ibyari adds يا ويلتى to the words of lament and quotes al-Naḥḥās as preferring to leave hāʾ al-sakt in some categories; his numbering there is unclear. The scholars' difference over من كيدكن (12:28) is reported by the Durrah study without a single ruling.

Hāʾ al-kināyah: the Durrah study announces seven words read without ṣilah but lists eight (including فيه مهانا). For بيده it gives four places (2:237, 2:249, 23:88, 36:83); El-Ibyari lists three, without 2:237.
Waqf on مال (4:78, 18:49, 25:7, 70:36): the Durrah study says Yaʿqūb stops on the lām, then adds that Ibn al-Jazarī allows a stop on either letter for all ten readers.
Count of yāʾāt al-zawāʾid: the table in the Durrah study has 123 rows, two of which (12:12, 12:90) are marked as not his; rules-of-the-10-qiraat counts 117. No total is stated in the chapter.

Verse references corrected from garbled or differing numbers in the sources: هل ترى 67:3 (printed 'al-Mulk 79'), يرد ثواب 3:145 (printed 3:176), ثم تتفكروا 34:46 (a footnote prints al-Muʾminūn 101), يضاهون 9:30 (printed 9:110), أأذهبتم 46:20 (printed 'al-Aḥqāf 113' and 46:19), واد النمل 27:18, عادا الأولى 53:50 and من إستبرق 55:54 (El-Ibyari prints 53:49 and 55:52), دكا 18:98 (El-Ibyari prints 18:94).

Left out as unclear: El-Ibyari's addition of أن يؤتى أحد (3:73) to the words Yaʿqūb reads as a question (not in the Durrah study), his passage on ءآلذكرين / ءآلله / ءآلآن, and most of his farsh word list, whose Arabic is too garbled in the extracted text to read safely.

The Durrah study glosses the dropping (ḥadhf) of the alif of أنا before a hamzah with the word 'affirmation'; it is taken here as dropping the alif in waṣl. The stop with hāʾ on the feminine tāʾ written open comes from El-Ibyari (p. 311); the Durrah study mentions only يا أبت.
